intro: Why do we say “I know” and never “I'm knowing”, but “I'm thinking about it” next to “I think so”? Some verbs describe a state (an opinion, knowledge, possession, feelings) and normally do not take the continuous form; others change their meaning with the form. This is a constant source of mistakes.
objectifs: Recognise the main groups of state verbs (thoughts, feelings, possession, senses, description).
Distinguish the two meanings of think, have, see, taste, smell, look, weigh, be…
Use “can see / can hear” and sense verbs followed by an adjective (It smells good).
Understand modern uses (“I'm loving it”, “I'm hoping…”) and the rule in other tenses.

texte: An action (dynamic) verb describes something that happens, that starts and finishes: run, eat, write, cook. It can take the continuous form: “I'm cooking.”

A state (stative) verb describes a situation, a thought, a feeling or possession: there is no activity in progress. We normally use the simple form, even for the present moment: “I know the answer”, “She owns two shops”, “This book belongs to me”.
Ask yourself: is something happening, or is something simply true?

lignes: know, believe, understand, remember, forget, realise, suppose, mean, think (= have an opinion)
like, love, hate, prefer, want, need, wish, mind
This car belongs to my uncle.
be, seem, appear, look (= seem), consist, contain, cost, weigh, depend, matter, deserve

texte: Several verbs are state verbs with one meaning and action verbs with another. The meaning decides the form, not the verb itself.
The most common case is “think”: “I think it's a good idea” (opinion, state); “I'm thinking about changing jobs” (considering, a mental activity).
“Have” meaning possess or have a characteristic stays simple; in action expressions (have breakfast, have a shower, have a party, have fun, have a baby), it can be continuous.

lignes: I'm seeing the doctor at 3. (meeting) / She's seeing someone. (dating)
The soup tastes salty. (has a flavour)
The chef is tasting the soup. (trying it)
The kitchen smells of garlic. (has a smell)
Why are you smelling the milk? (sniffing)
The nurse is weighing the baby. (action)
She's appearing in a new film. (acting)

texte: For an involuntary perception at the present moment, British English very often uses “can”: “I can see the sea from my window”, “Can you hear that noise?”. “I'm seeing the sea” is wrong.

Look, sound, smell, taste and feel can be followed by an adjective (not an adverb), like “be”: “This cake smells delicious”, “Your idea sounds great”, “You look tired”. Say “it smells good”, not “well”.
You can also use “like” + noun: “It looks like rain”, “It sounds like a good plan”.
exemples: I can hear someone in the garden.
This fish smells strange. Don't eat it.
It looks like it's going to rain.

texte: “Be” is normally a state verb, but “be being + adjective” describes temporary, often unusual behaviour: “He's a kind person” (character); “You're being very rude today” (your behaviour now). Common adjectives: silly, rude, difficult, careful, kind, honest, lazy.

“Feel” for a sensation or physical state accepts both forms: “I feel tired / I'm feeling tired”. The -ing form stresses the moment. Meaning “have an opinion”, it stays simple: “I feel (that) we should wait.”
The same goes for “hurt” and “ache”: “My back hurts / My back is hurting”.
exemples: Common question from a doctor or friend.
I feel that we need more time.

texte: In informal speech and advertising, you hear “I'm loving it”, “I'm liking this new job”: the -ing form shows enthusiasm or a current impression. It is accepted in speech, but avoid it in careful writing or exams.
“I'm hoping”, “I'm wondering” and “I was wondering” are very common polite phrases: “I was wondering if you could help me.” They soften a request.

The rule applies in all tenses: no continuous form with a state verb in the present perfect, the past or the future. “I've known her for years” (not “I've been knowing”), “I didn't understand” (not “I wasn't understanding”), “I'll need help” (not “I'll be needing”, except in some very polite uses).
exemples: I was wondering if you could send me the file.
I'm hoping to finish by Friday.
A careful way to express hope.
I've always believed in hard work.

formule: State verb → simple form (I know, it belongs, it tastes good) · Action meaning → continuous possible (I'm thinking about it, she's having lunch)
prononciation: “tastes” /teɪsts/ and “costs” /kɒsts/: pronounce the whole final consonant group, without adding a vowel.
Contrastive stress: “You're BEING rude” highlights the temporary behaviour.
“I can see”: “can” is weak, /kən/; in the negative “can't” /kɑːnt/ is stressed.
“I was wondering”: a soft falling intonation, polite tone: /aɪ wəz ˈwʌndərɪŋ/.
erreurs: think (= have an opinion): simple form.
After smell / taste / look / sound: adjective.
I'm seeing the sea from my window.
I can see the sea from my window.

dialogue.contexte: In Abidjan, during the filming of a cooking show. Chef Aya is preparing grilled fish with her assistant, Kévin.
lignes: Kévin, what are you doing? Are you tasting my sauce already?
Sorry, chef! But it smells amazing. I can smell the ginger from here.
It tastes perfect. I think it needs a little more salt, though.
You're being very honest today! OK, I'm thinking about it…
The fish weighs almost two kilos. Do you want me to cut it?
Yes, please. And the attiéké? Does it contain enough oil?
It looks good to me. Everyone in the studio is having a great time!
look: seem; have a great time: action.

mots: This sauce tastes a bit spicy.
to have a particular flavour; to try food
The kitchen smells of fresh bread.
to have a particular smell; a smell
They own a small hotel in Kribi.
to have something that is legally yours
Who does this phone belong to?
to be the property of someone
This drink contains a lot of sugar.
to change according to something else
She seems happy in her new job.
to like one thing more than another
to have earned something because of your actions

items: We (have / are having) dinner at the moment.

exercices.consigne: Put the verb into the present simple or present continuous.
items: What ___ you ___ (think) of my new haircut?
She ___ (see) a lawyer this afternoon about the contract.
Why ___ you ___ (be) so rude today? You're not usually like this.
I ___ (not / understand) this sentence. Can you explain it?
The chef ___ (taste) the soup to check the salt.

exercices.consigne: Explain the difference in meaning between the two sentences.
items: I think it's a good idea. / I'm thinking about changing jobs.
She has a car. / She's having a shower.
I see what you mean. / I'm seeing my doctor tomorrow.
He's a difficult person. / He's being difficult.
The baby weighs 4 kilos. / The nurse is weighing the baby.

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: This bag is belonging to my sister.
This bag belongs to my sister.
I'm seeing the sea from my window.
I can see the sea from my window.

exercices.consigne: Make a sentence with the words given (sense verb + adjective).
items: You look tired today. (You're looking tired is also possible.)

exercices.consigne: Write 4–5 sentences about what you feel, think and do right now, using at least three verbs with two meanings (think, have, see, taste, look…) in both uses.
items: I'm having a quiet evening at home. I'm thinking about my holiday plans, but I think I'll stay in Belgium this year. My sister is seeing a new doctor, and she looks much better. The tea I'm drinking tastes of mint, and it smells wonderful.

a_retenir: State verbs (know, believe, like, want, own, belong, seem, contain, cost…): simple form, even for now.
Verbs with two meanings: think, have, see, taste, smell, look, weigh, appear — the meaning decides.
Involuntary perception: I can see / I can hear; look / smell / taste / sound + adjective.
be being + adjective = temporary behaviour; feel / hurt: both forms possible.
“I'm loving it” is informal; “I was wondering if…” is a polite formula.
